title: What should you ask first in a cost or operations case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a cost and operations case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Cost and operations cases are about doing the same work for less, or doing it better. Here is where to start.
body:
The first question to ask

Goal: lower cost, more capacity, or reliability?

How to build your structure

  1. Map the cost base: what are the biggest lines?
  2. Benchmark each line against peers to find the biggest gap
  3. Start with the biggest gap
  4. List levers: people, process, technology, suppliers
  5. Check what each cut would do to revenue and quality

The trap most people fall into

Cutting costs that carry revenue.

For the full tree, with every branch, read the cost reduction framework.

Two prompts to try

A telecom company's customer complaints have tripled in six months.

Show a model structure
  • What they complain about: Billing, network, installation, support; Which category grew
  • Who complains: New vs existing customers; Region, product, channel they joined through
  • What changed: New billing system, price rise, outsourcing; Timing vs the rise
  • How we handle them: First-call resolution; Time to fix, repeat complaints

Where to start: What changed six months ago: a tripling rarely happens without a trigger.

The trap: Hiring more call-centre staff before finding the cause.

A furniture factory's defect rate rose from 2% to 6%.

Show a model structure
  • Where defects appear: Which product, line and process step; Which shift
  • Materials: Supplier changes, wood quality; Storage and humidity
  • People: New or temporary staff, training; Overtime and fatigue
  • Machines and process: Maintenance, settings, wear; New equipment or faster line speed

Where to start: Where defects appear: narrowing to one step usually reveals the cause.

The trap: Adding more inspection at the end instead of fixing the cause.

Find the constraint before automating

An online grocery warehouse processes 600 orders a day. Picking can handle 750 orders, packing 620 and dispatch 580. Without other bottlenecks, the entire system's sustainable throughput is capped near 580 orders per day by dispatch, not picking.

Investing in faster picking equipment may make the picking stage impressive while the overall delivery promise gets worse. First draw the process from receiving the order through dispatch. Measure arrival rates, throughput, error rates, queue size and peak demand at each step.

If a dispatch change lifts capacity to 680 orders a day, packing at 620 becomes the next bottleneck. That is normal. Operations improvement is iterative: fix the binding constraint, measure end-to-end performance, then repeat. Include customer service and safety, not just unit cost.
